LLM auditresponse for .SRCINFO:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is the `.SRCINFO` metadata file for `gapcode-bin`, an unofficial package for the GapGPT AI coding agent. It contains only standard packaging metadata: version, description, architectures, licenses, dependencies, and sources.

The binary tarballs are fetched over `https` from `gapgpt.ir` and both the x86_64 and aarch64 sources have pinned `sha256sums` (not SKIP), which is good practice. There are no shell commands, no `eval`/`base64`/`curl|bash`, no obfuscation, and no unexpected file operations present in this file — it is pure metadata.

One minor hygiene observation: the declared project URL is `https://gapgpt.app` while the release binaries are downloaded from `https://gapgpt.ir`. This domain discrepancy is worth noting for verification purposes, but on its own it is not evidence of malicious behavior — it may simply reflect the upstream's distribution host. No exfiltration, backdoor, or code-execution indicators were found.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Metadata-only SRCINFO; pinned checksums, no malicious indicators.</summary>
</security_assessment>

[1/3] Reviewing PKGBUILD, gapcode.sh...
+ Reviewed .SRCINFO. Status: SAFE -- Metadata-only SRCINFO; pinned checksums, no malicious indicators.
LLM auditresponse for gapcode.sh:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This file (`gapcode.sh`) is a launcher wrapper for the GapCode application. Its logic is straightforward and self-consistent with its stated purpose:

1. It resolves a per-user home directory (`$GAPCODE_HOME` or `$HOME/.gapcode`).
2. If the background app-server daemon binary is missing at the expected per-user path but the path is either a dangling symlink or nonexistent, it creates a symlink at `packages/app-server-daemon/current` pointing to `/opt/gapcode` (the packaged system install). This is a legitimate workaround for the daemon-path issue described in the comments.
3. It `exec`s the packaged binary `/opt/gapcode/bin/codex`, forwarding all arguments and setting `argv[0]` to `gapcode`.

I found no red flags: there are no network requests or downloads (no `curl`/`wget`), no obfuscation or encoding, no `eval` of decoded blobs, and no file operations targeting data outside the application's own scope. All filesystem writes are confined to the user's own `.gapcode` directory and point only at the packaged install location (`/opt/gapcode`). The symlink target and executed binary are the package's own upstream code, which is expected behavior for a launcher wrapper. Error redirection (`2>/dev/null`) and quoted variable expansions are consistent with defensive, ordinary packaging practice.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Benign launcher wrapper; no malicious behavior detected.</summary>
</security_assessment>

The file is a standard Arch PKGBUILD for a prebuilt binary package. It declares versioned upstream release artifacts and checksums, then uses ordinary packaging commands such as install, cp, and find in the package function. There is no evidence of obfuscated code, eval, base64 decoding, curl or wget execution, network exfiltration, backdoor, or download-and-run behavior.

The source handling and installation flow are consistent with an unofficial package wrapping an upstream application. No genuinely malicious or injected behavior was found. Minor hygiene concerns, such as unclear source handling for the local gapcode.sh wrapper, do not by themselves indicate a supply-chain attack.
</details>
<evidence></evidence>
